screens.title: The Liskov Substitution Principle
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the Liskov Substitution Principle, a core idea in object-oriented design about behavior, not just structure. LSP says that when code expects an instance of a base type, supplying a subtype should not change the correctness of the program. That means subclasses must honor the same observable contract — inputs, outputs, side effects, and exceptions — that clients rely on. You will see why this is a stronger requirement than simply sharing method names, and why failing to respect it creates surprising runtime errors and brittle hierarchies. We will study familiar counterexamples — rectangles and squares, birds and penguins — and then practice a refactor that removes an LSP violation by introducing a capability interface. Along the way we will clarify terms: behavioral subtyping, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, and discuss when composition is a safer choice than inheritance. By the end you should be able to spot an LSP violation, explain why it matters for maintainability and testing, and choose a refactoring that preserves substitutability. Think about a recent inheritance you wrote: could a client be surprised if a subclass changed the expected behavior?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: LSP requires that subtypes preserve the behavioral contract of their supertypes so client code can use any subtype without changing correctness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Liskov Substitution Principle

Why subclasses must behave like their supertypes so programs remain correct and extensible.

This chapter focuses on behavioral contracts and refactor patterns that preserve substitutability.
What you'll learn
  • What LSP requires beyond method signatures.
  • Common violations and how they show up at runtime.
  • Refactor strategies: interfaces, abstract base classes, and composition.
Concept Map
Behavioral Contract
Contract = preconditions, postconditions, invariants, side effects and exceptions that clients rely upon.
Subtypes must not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or introduce unexpected failures.
When violated, substitution causes runtime surprises, brittle tests, and maintenance cost.
Explore Key Topics
Rectangle & Square
A classic violation: identical structure, different behavior.
Birds & Penguins
When a subclass cannot perform a base class capability, prefer interfaces.
Refactor Activity
Refactor Vehicle/Car/Bicycle to introduce a Refuelable contract.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will clearly distinguish structural compatibility from behavioral substitutability. First, you will understand the formal idea of LSP: a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking program correctness. Second, you will identify common real-world patterns that break that rule — for example, subclasses that change expected side effects, introduce new exceptions, or alter method postconditions. Third, you will practice refactoring a hierarchy that violates LSP by introducing capability interfaces or abstract base classes so that clients depend on what they use, not on concrete types. Finally, you will learn to choose composition over inheritance when the relationship is "uses-a" rather than "is-a." Each objective emphasizes why the skill matters: preserving substitutability reduces runtime surprises, simplifies testing, and enables safe extension of code without changing clients. As you learn, test yourself by asking if a client could replace a base instance with a subtype and still reason about behavior. That simple question is a reliable LSP check.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Checks
screens.narratorSegment: This screen gives practical checks you can apply while designing or reviewing code. First, ask whether a client that expects the base type could substitute any subclass without modifying its logic. Second, list the method contracts: what are the preconditions, what are the postconditions, and what invariants must hold? Third, ensure subclasses do not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions — doing so breaks substitutability. Fourth, prefer composition or capability interfaces if a subtype cannot fulfill the base contract. For each check, practice by reading a method signature and imagining a client call that relies on a particular behavior. A useful refactor pattern is turning a method-based capability into an explicit interface or abstract base class so clients declare dependence on capability rather than concrete type. These checks are short but powerful: they catch LSP violations early, keep tests robust, and reduce surprises when new subclasses arrive. Use them whenever you introduce inheritance or modify a base class contract.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Practice Checks

Design checks for LSP

Short heuristics to use during reviews and refactors.

Substitution Question

Could client code be given any subtype and keep working correctly? If not, identify the behavior mismatch.

Contract Checklist

List preconditions, postconditions, invariants, and allowed exceptions for each method the client relies on.

Refactor Tools

Introduce capability interfaces, abstract base classes, or use composition to isolate differing behavior.

Testing Strategy

Test components against base-type expectations so any compatible subtype will pass existing tests.

screens.title: What LSP means: behavioral subtyping
screens.narratorSegment: LSP is best understood as a requirement about observable behavior. When a client depends on a base type, that client has expectations about how methods behave: what arguments are allowed, what the method returns, what side effects happen, and what exceptions may be raised. A subtype must honor all those expectations. In formal terms, a subtype must not strengthen preconditions — it cannot demand more from a caller than the base did — and it must not weaken postconditions — it must deliver at least the promised results. It must preserve invariants that clients depend on. A concrete example: if a base class method promises to never raise a certain exception on valid input, a subclass cannot start raising it for those same inputs. The practical effect is predictability: clients can reason about code using the base type, and new subtypes will not invalidate those assumptions. A common misconception is to equate LSP with having identical method signatures. That is necessary but not sufficient. Structure matters for compilation; LSP guards runtime contracts that keep systems correct and testable. Ask yourself: does substituting a subtype change what a client can expect? If yes, you have an LSP issue.

keyIdea.title: Behavioral subtyping
keyIdea.text: Subtypes must preserve preconditions, postconditions, and invariants so clients can use them interchangeably.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Behavioral Subtyping
Definition

LSP as a behavioral contract

Preconditions: requirements the caller must meet. Subtypes must not require more.
Postconditions: guarantees after a method runs. Subtypes must provide at least the same guarantees.
Invariants: persistent truths about object state that must hold across operations.
Key Takeaway

Behavior matters more than shape; substitution must preserve observable guarantees.

Common misconception

Matching method signatures is insufficient; a subclass can still violate client expectations by changing behavior.

Concrete example
Imagine a base class method that returns a positive integer and never raises an error for valid input. If a subclass starts raising errors for those same inputs, client code that relied on a successful return path will fail. That is an LSP violation.
Check to apply
  • List the base method's expected inputs and outputs.
  • Confirm the subclass preserves those expectations.
  • If it cannot, refactor to an interface or composition.

screens.title: Rectangle vs Square: A classic LSP trap
screens.narratorSegment: The Rectangle and Square example shows how structural inheritance can hide behavioral mismatch. A rectangle exposes set_width and set_height; a square enforces equal sides. If Square inherits Rectangle and overrides setters to maintain its invariant, client code that expects independent width and height will see different behavior. For instance, a function that sets width to 10 and height to 5 expects the area to be fifty; with a Square that enforces equality, the final state is ambiguous or incorrect relative to that expectation. This breaks substitutability because clients rely on the rectangle's contract of independent dimensions. The lesson is about intent: is a square really a special rectangle in terms of the operations you need? If not, inheritance is the wrong tool. A correct model keeps the independent-dimensions contract on Rectangle, and represents squares either as a separate type or as a factory that constructs a Rectangle with equal sides without inheriting. A common remedy is to extract shared behavior into a separate component used by both shapes, or to provide immutable value objects that represent dimensions, avoiding setter-based invariants that create surprises.

keyIdea.text: When subtype behavior alters base expectations—like independent setters—substitution fails; model intent explicitly instead.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Rectangle vs Square
Problem

Square inherits Rectangle

Setters that once operated independently now must preserve an invariant, breaking client expectations.

Misleading similarity
Both have width and height, but their operational contracts differ.
Better options
Separate types, composition, or immutable value objects avoid setter surprises.
Example scenario
A layout routine that adjusts width and height independently will miscalculate areas or break when a square enforces equality.
Visual comparison
Rectangle
  • set_width(w) independent
  • set_height(h) independent
  • Clients expect independent resize
Square (subclass)
  • enforces width == height
  • setters adjust both values
  • Breaks rectangle client assumptions
Check your understanding

If client code relies on independent setters, would substituting a Square be safe? Reflect on the answer.

screens.title: Preconditions, Postconditions & Invariants
screens.narratorSegment: LSP is expressed in contract terms: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. A precondition is what a method requires from its caller — inputs must satisfy certain constraints. If a subtype strengthens a precondition, some callers that were valid for the base will fail for the subtype. A postcondition is what the method guarantees after running. Weakening postconditions means the caller cannot rely on previously promised results. Invariants are truths that must hold for the object's state across operations; violating invariants in a subtype can cause subtle errors. Consider exceptions: if a subclass starts raising new exceptions on inputs that the base accepted, clients that didn't handle those exceptions will break at runtime. A useful way to think about this is substitution tests: pick a client scenario that uses the base type and replace it with the subtype. Does the scenario still complete correctly? If not, a contract element changed. Documenting method contracts explicitly — in comments, tests, or type annotations — makes violations easier to spot. This contract viewpoint turns LSP from an abstract rule into concrete checks you can perform during design and code review.

keyIdea.title: Contract language
keyIdea.text: Check preconditions, postconditions, and invariants to validate substitutability and avoid hidden runtime surprises.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Contracts

Preconditions

Requirements callers must satisfy before invoking a method.

Example: a method that accepts a positive integer has a precondition that the input is positive.
Violation: a subtype rejects zero or negative values the base accepted, breaking callers.
Design tip
Keep preconditions as weak as possible; avoid forcing callers to meet stricter requirements in subtypes.

Postconditions & Invariants

Postconditions state what is true after the call; invariants hold across method calls.

Example: a method promises to return a non-null object; weakening this promise in a subtype will surprise callers.
Invariant example: object coordinates remain non-negative. A subtype must preserve that truth or clients fail unexpectedly.
Quick check
Run substitution tests: execute client scenarios with the subtype and verify contracts hold.

screens.title: Bird & Penguin: runtime surprise in Python
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Bird and Penguin example in Python to see how LSP violations surface at runtime. In the simplest design, Bird defines a fly method that prints or performs flying behavior. Penguin inherits from Bird but cannot fly. If Penguin overrides fly to raise a not implemented error or to do nothing, any client that expects a bird to fly will either crash or silently miss behavior. This is a direct violation: the base contract promises fly works for valid Bird instances. The remedy is to separate capability from generalization. Introduce a Flyable interface or abstract base class that declares fly as a capability. FlyingBird implements Flyable; NonFlyingBird or Penguin does not. Then client code that needs flying depends explicitly on Flyable. That change moves the expectation to a type the client can rely on at design time, avoiding runtime surprises. Tests also become clearer: testing code that calls fly only requires a Flyable test double, not every bird. This approach makes intent explicit and keeps inheritance for true "is-a" cases only. Bird & Penguin: runtime surprise in Python means if a subclass cannot provide a capability the base promises, model that capability explicitly and avoid false inheritance.. In practical terms, a concrete python example that highlights a violation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bird/Penguin example
keyIdea.text: If a subclass cannot provide a capability the base promises, model that capability explicitly and avoid false inheritance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Bird / Penguin
Example code (simplified)
class Bird:
    def fly(self):
        print("Bird is flying high!")

class Penguin(Bird):
    def fly(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("Penguins cannot fly!")

def make_bird_fly(bird: Bird):
    try:
        bird.fly()
    except NotImplementedError as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}")

make_bird_fly(Bird())
make_bird_fly(Penguin())
This code leads to a runtime error for Penguins when clients expected flying behavior. The fix is to make flying an explicit capability.
Refactor idea
Introduce Flyable
Define a Flyable interface or abstract base and have only flying birds implement it. Clients that need flying accept Flyable, not Bird.
Testing benefit
Clients that call fly can be tested with Flyable mocks, keeping tests focused and avoiding Penguin surprises.

screens.title: Detecting LSP violations during review
screens.narratorSegment: Spotting LSP violations early makes maintenance far easier. Use this checklist as a deterministic process during reviews. First, identify any new inheritance relationships. For each, ask the substitution question: can any client using the base type accept the new subtype without changing behavior? Second, list the base methods relied on by clients and document their expected inputs, outputs, side effects, and exceptions. Third, inspect overridden methods in the subtype: ensure they do not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or introduce new error modes. Fourth, run substitution tests: run representative client scenarios replacing the base with the subtype. Fifth, when a subtype cannot satisfy the contract, prefer composition or an explicit capability interface. Finally, add tests that assert contractual behavior so future refactors will fail fast if substitution is broken. Applying this flow means you treat LSP violations like failing tests rather than emergent runtime surprises, turning an abstract principle into a repeatable engineering practice. Detecting LSP violations during review means use a substitution question, contract listing, override inspection, substitution tests, and refactor to interfaces or composition when needed.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Review Checklist

Detect LSP violations

A step-by-step process you can follow in every design or code review.

1
Substitution question
Can a client using the base type accept the subtype unchanged?
2
List method contracts
Record preconditions, postconditions, side effects, and allowed exceptions.
3
Inspect overrides
Ensure overrides don't require more or promise less than the base methods.
4
Run substitution tests
Execute representative client scenarios using the subtype in place of the base.
5
Refactor if needed
If the subtype cannot satisfy the contract, prefer composition or explicit capability interfaces.
Why this helps
Turning LSP into a checklist converts an abstract principle into concrete engineering steps that catch surprises early.

screens.title: Prefer capability interfaces and composition
screens.narratorSegment: When a subtype cannot satisfy a base type's behavior, capability interfaces and composition provide clean alternatives. Capability interfaces declare a specific action — for example, Refuelable or Flyable — and only types that support that action implement it. This makes client dependencies explicit: code that needs refueling depends on Refuelable, not Vehicle. Composition moves shared behavior into a contained object that types can use without pretending to be one another. For instance, instead of making Bicycle inherit from Vehicle and suffer a forced refuel method, create a Refuelable mixin or a separate FuelTank component and only attach it to vehicles that truly use fuel. Composition also aligns with single responsibility: the fuel-related logic lives in a focused component and can be tested independently. These approaches preserve LSP by preventing the introduction of contracts that some subtypes cannot keep. They also improve testability and future extension because new capabilities are opt-in, not mandated by an inheritance chain. Prefer capability interfaces and composition means use capability interfaces or composition to model optional behaviors so clients depend only on what they use.. In practical terms, design patterns that keep substitutability explicit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interfaces & composition
keyIdea.text: Use capability interfaces or composition to model optional behaviors so clients depend only on what they use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Interfaces & Composition

Capability interfaces

Define an interface for the exact capability a client needs, and have only supporting types implement it.

Example
Refuelable: an interface with refuel. Car implements it, Bicycle does not.
Benefit
Clients express explicit capability dependencies and avoid false substitution.

Composition

Extract shared functionality into components used by types that need it, instead of forcing inheritance.

FuelTank component
Attach to Car, not to Bicycle. Tests target FuelTank behavior separately.
Design tip
Use composition when behavior is optional or orthogonal to the base type's identity.

screens.title: Refactor Vehicle/Car/Bicycle to comply with LSP
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough presents a refactor from the chapter's starter code. The original design made Bicycle inherit from Vehicle and forced a refuel method on all vehicles. That is an LSP violation: a bicycle does not require refueling and will break client code that expects refuel to work. The refactor introduces a Refuelable interface or abstract base that declares refuel. Car implements Refuelable; Bicycle does not. The service routine is changed to accept only Refuelable vehicles. This preserves substitutability because every object passed to the service actually supports the required behavior. The design also improves clarity: client code now documents its capabilities, tests become explicit, and the inheritance hierarchy no longer misrepresents the real relationships. Implementing the change involves extracting refuel into a separate contract, updating Car to implement it, and changing service_vehicle signature and tests to accept Refuelable. This small change removes runtime surprises and aligns the model with real-world behavior. Refactor Vehicle/Car/Bicycle to comply with LSP means extract the refuel behavior into a refuelable contract and have only refuelable types implement it; update clients to depend on that interface.. In practical terms, introduce refuelable so clients depend on capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Vehicle Refactor
Starter code problem
class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, fuel_level):
        self.fuel_level = fuel_level

    def refuel(self, amount):
        self.fuel_level += amount

class Car(Vehicle):
    pass

class Bicycle(Vehicle):
    def __init__(self, gear_count):
        super().__init__(0)
    def refuel(self, amount):
        raise NotImplementedError("Bicycles do not require refueling!")
This design forces Bicycle to inherit a refuel contract it cannot satisfy, causing service routines to fail if a bicycle is passed.
Refactored approach
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Refuelable(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def refuel(self, amount):
        pass

class Car(Refuelable):
    def __init__(self, fuel_level):
        self.fuel_level = fuel_level
    def refuel(self, amount):
        self.fuel_level += amount

class Bicycle:
    def __init__(self, gear_count):
        self.gear_count = gear_count
Now service routines accept Refuelable and will only be given objects that support refuel, eliminating the violation.

screens.title: When inheritance is appropriate
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is valuable when a subclass truly is a more specific kind of its superclass, both in structure and behavior. Ask: does the subtype promise all behaviors clients expect from the base? If yes, inheritance can express that relationship naturally. If the subtype only reuses code but cannot or should not satisfy the base contract, then inheritance is dangerous. Consider a utility that shares algorithms or helpers; composition achieves that reuse without forcing substitutability. Another practical guideline is to design base classes for extension: document the contract and expected behaviors clearly so implementers know what to preserve. When designing frameworks or libraries, provide abstract base classes that declare invariants and document expected exception behavior. If you find yourself writing defensive checks or conditional logic in the base to accommodate divergent subclass behavior, that is a smell indicating inheritance is being misused. Use composition to assemble behaviors, and reserve inheritance for true specialization that preserves the base contract. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › When to Inherit

True "is-a" relationships

The subclass must preserve both shape and behavioral promises of the base type.

If subclass requires new preconditions, avoid inheritance.
If subclass introduces new failure modes unseen by base, avoid inheritance.
When behavior aligns, inheritance expresses clear specialization and is appropriate.

Code reuse vs. substitutability

If you only need shared implementation, prefer composition to avoid forcing contract obligations.

Design smell
Base classes containing conditional logic for subclasses often indicate misuse of inheritance.

screens.title: Common LSP violations and how they appear
screens.narratorSegment: LSP violations typically appear as one of a few patterns. First, subclasses introducing new exceptions for inputs the base accepted breaks callers that do not handle them. Second, changing return types or weakening postconditions causes clients to receive unexpected results. Third, altering side effects — for instance, modifying shared state in ways the base didn't — produces subtle bugs. Fourth, strengthening preconditions makes previously valid client calls invalid for the subtype. The chapter's examples illustrate these: Pengiun raises an exception when fly is called, Square changes setter semantics, and Bicycle inherits a refuel method it cannot meaningfully implement. Detecting these problems requires reading both client expectations and overridden implementations. The engineering remedy is predictable: either make the capability explicit via an interface, extract behavior into composition, or redesign the base class so it does not promise operations that all descendants cannot keep. Adding focused tests that assert expected exceptions and side effects guards against regressions and documents the contract for future implementers. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the Liskov Substitution Principle, a core idea in object-oriented design about behavior, not just structure. LSP says that when code expects an instance of a base type, supplying a subtype should not change the correctness of the program. That means subclasses must honor the same observable contract — inputs, outputs, side effects, and exceptions — that clients rely on. You will see why this is a stronger requirement than simply sharing method names, and why failing to respect it creates surprising runtime errors and brittle hierarchies. We will study familiar counterexamples — rectangles and squares, birds and penguins — and then practice a refactor that removes an LSP violation by introducing a capability interface. Along the way we will clarify terms: behavioral subtyping, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, and discuss when composition is a safer choice than inheritance. By the end you should be able to spot an LSP violation, explain why it matters for maintainability and testing, and choose a refactoring that preserves substitutability. Think about a recent inheritance you wrote: could a client be surprised if a subclass changed the expected behavior?

By the end of these screens you will clearly distinguish structural compatibility from behavioral substitutability. First, you will understand the formal idea of LSP: a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking program correctness. Second, you will identify common real-world patterns that break that rule — for example, subclasses that change expected side effects, introduce new exceptions, or alter method postconditions. Third, you will practice refactoring a hierarchy that violates LSP by introducing capability interfaces or abstract base classes so that clients depend on what they use, not on concrete types. Finally, you will learn to choose composition over inheritance when the relationship is "uses-a" rather than "is-a." Each objective emphasizes why the skill matters: preserving substitutability reduces runtime surprises, simplifies testing, and enables safe extension of code without changing clients. As you learn, test yourself by asking if a client could replace a base instance with a subtype and still reason about behavior. That simple question is a reliable LSP check.

This screen gives practical checks you can apply while designing or reviewing code. First, ask whether a client that expects the base type could substitute any subclass without modifying its logic. Second, list the method contracts: what are the preconditions, what are the postconditions, and what invariants must hold? Third, ensure subclasses do not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions — doing so breaks substitutability. Fourth, prefer composition or capability interfaces if a subtype cannot fulfill the base contract. For each check, practice by reading a method signature and imagining a client call that relies on a particular behavior. A useful refactor pattern is turning a method-based capability into an explicit interface or abstract base class so clients declare dependence on capability rather than concrete type. These checks are short but powerful: they catch LSP violations early, keep tests robust, and reduce surprises when new subclasses arrive. Use them whenever you introduce inheritance or modify a base class contract.

LSP is best understood as a requirement about observable behavior. When a client depends on a base type, that client has expectations about how methods behave: what arguments are allowed, what the method returns, what side effects happen, and what exceptions may be raised. A subtype must honor all those expectations. In formal terms, a subtype must not strengthen preconditions — it cannot demand more from a caller than the base did — and it must not weaken postconditions — it must deliver at least the promised results. It must preserve invariants that clients depend on. A concrete example: if a base class method promises to never raise a certain exception on valid input, a subclass cannot start raising it for those same inputs. The practical effect is predictability: clients can reason about code using the base type, and new subtypes will not invalidate those assumptions. A common misconception is to equate LSP with having identical method signatures. That is necessary but not sufficient. Structure matters for compilation; LSP guards runtime contracts that keep systems correct and testable. Ask yourself: does substituting a subtype change what a client can expect? If yes, you have an LSP issue.

The Rectangle and Square example shows how structural inheritance can hide behavioral mismatch. A rectangle exposes set_width and set_height; a square enforces equal sides. If Square inherits Rectangle and overrides setters to maintain its invariant, client code that expects independent width and height will see different behavior. For instance, a function that sets width to 10 and height to 5 expects the area to be fifty; with a Square that enforces equality, the final state is ambiguous or incorrect relative to that expectation. This breaks substitutability because clients rely on the rectangle's contract of independent dimensions. The lesson is about intent: is a square really a special rectangle in terms of the operations you need? If not, inheritance is the wrong tool. A correct model keeps the independent-dimensions contract on Rectangle, and represents squares either as a separate type or as a factory that constructs a Rectangle with equal sides without inheriting. A common remedy is to extract shared behavior into a separate component used by both shapes, or to provide immutable value objects that represent dimensions, avoiding setter-based invariants that create surprises.

LSP is expressed in contract terms: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. A precondition is what a method requires from its caller — inputs must satisfy certain constraints. If a subtype strengthens a precondition, some callers that were valid for the base will fail for the subtype. A postcondition is what the method guarantees after running. Weakening postconditions means the caller cannot rely on previously promised results. Invariants are truths that must hold for the object's state across operations; violating invariants in a subtype can cause subtle errors. Consider exceptions: if a subclass starts raising new exceptions on inputs that the base accepted, clients that didn't handle those exceptions will break at runtime. A useful way to think about this is substitution tests: pick a client scenario that uses the base type and replace it with the subtype. Does the scenario still complete correctly? If not, a contract element changed. Documenting method contracts explicitly — in comments, tests, or type annotations — makes violations easier to spot. This contract viewpoint turns LSP from an abstract rule into concrete checks you can perform during design and code review.

Let's walk through the Bird and Penguin example in Python to see how LSP violations surface at runtime. In the simplest design, Bird defines a fly method that prints or performs flying behavior. Penguin inherits from Bird but cannot fly. If Penguin overrides fly to raise a not implemented error or to do nothing, any client that expects a bird to fly will either crash or silently miss behavior. This is a direct violation: the base contract promises fly works for valid Bird instances. The remedy is to separate capability from generalization. Introduce a Flyable interface or abstract base class that declares fly as a capability. FlyingBird implements Flyable; NonFlyingBird or Penguin does not. Then client code that needs flying depends explicitly on Flyable. That change moves the expectation to a type the client can rely on at design time, avoiding runtime surprises. Tests also become clearer: testing code that calls fly only requires a Flyable test double, not every bird. This approach makes intent explicit and keeps inheritance for true "is-a" cases only. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
